« On ne partira pas » – Mobilisation à C: “We’re not leaving” – Chameran residents mobilize against a “possible renoviction”
À Saint-Laurent, des locataires dénoncen: In Saint-Laurent, tenants are denouncing a renoviction and organizing to stay in buildings they describe as unfit for habitation.

Half-empty, dilapidated buildings in Chameran, where a swimming pool abandoned for years symbolizes the decay tenants are denouncing.

J’ai pris connaissance de ce dossier grâ: I first heard about this story from two Chameran residents who came to our offices to share their concerns, and I then learned more from posts by activist groups. What caught my attention wasn’t only the word “renoviction,” but the gap between what was being said and what it actually meant for families, in a neighbourhood that gets little media coverage, like Chameran.
Je suis allé voir. J’ai rencontré des pe: I went to see for myself. I met people involved in the mobilization, then visited the buildings, spoke with tenants and looked at the units. What I saw matched descriptions in existing municipal documents, but it took on a different dimension once I was on the ground.
Ce sujet s’inscrit dans ce que l’on couv: This story is part of what we cover at La Converse: local situations rooted in neighbourhoods where larger issues like housing, inequality and urban transformation play out. Here, it isn’t only about renovations or procedures, but about the ability to stay in your own home.
J’ai aussi cherché à obtenir la version: I also sought the side of the institutions and the landlord. I pressed to speak with the borough mayor. I contacted the landlord several times, but had still received no response from them at the time of publication.
Ce texte est le résultat de ce travail :: This article is the result of that work: starting from a faint signal, going to the scene, verifying, cross-checking and documenting what is at stake, as close as possible to the people living it.
<strong>À Chameran, dans l’arrondissemen: In Chameran, in the Saint-Laurent borough, tenants are refusing to leave their homes despite notices of major work that would relocate them as early as this summer. Many say they want to stay and are contesting these steps, which they see as a possible renoviction. On the ground, the buildings in question show signs of deterioration that have been documented for years, while rents have already risen sharply in neighbouring renovated buildings. Amid poor living conditions, a string of departures and collective organizing, a power struggle has emerged between residents, the landlord and local authorities.
Dans le vestibule du 1270, rue Quennevil: In the lobby of 1270 Quenneville Street, the conversation stops when an elderly woman steps out of the elevator and slowly approaches, a sheet of paper in her hand. In a barely audible voice, she asks whether her mover has arrived. The name and phone number are written in large letters, as if to hold on to a piece of information that has become essential. Her clothes bear the marks of everyday life, with no staging and no explanation. Marouane Cherifi, coordinator of the tenants’ defence committee, understands immediately: “That’s the third departure in a short time,” he says with a pang. One more in a building that is already largely empty. Here, people don’t always leave because of official notices; they also leave because of an accumulation of conditions that have become unbearable (constant work, noise, dust, uncertainty) and a diffuse pressure that ends up displacing the most vulnerable.
En janvier dernier, le propriétaire envo: Last January, the landlord sent out notice letters stating that “major renovations are necessary […] to ensure the safety of the occupants.” The form and content of the letter raised suspicions, and some residents consulted lawyers.
Dans ces immeubles, les familles et leur: In these buildings, families and their children live every day with the noise, the dust and the many inconveniences caused by the construction work. Photo: Nouri Nesrouche
C’est devant le 1315, rue Jules-Poitras: We begin our tour of this complex of five buildings (two on Quenneville Street and three on Jules-Poitras Street) in front of 1315 Jules-Poitras Street. The contrast is striking. Under a spring sun that gives the neighbourhood the feel of a village, the buildings hide a sordid reality. Only 1310 Quenneville Street, whose units have just been renovated and are awaiting new tenants, is an exception.
Dans les quatre autres immeubles, l’odeu: In the four other buildings, the smell of dampness hits you at the threshold of the apartments: walls swollen with water, crumbling ceilings, cockroaches showing up in kitchens, and all the rest! The City’s finding is unequivocal: seven major points of non-compliance, as one of the notices of non-compliance reviewed by La Converse indicates.
En avril 2025, l’ancien propriétaire, Ba: In April 2025, the former owner, Banvest, sold the five buildings to Orem Capital without meeting the City’s repair requirements. Tenants’ daily lives have continued amid unsanitary and unsafe conditions, and in recent months the disruption has been added to that. “I’ve lived here since 2019. And honestly, you wouldn’t think I’m in Canada! What I see here is stuff I wouldn’t even expect to see in a third-world country,” says Mr. Cherifi indignantly.
Dans les appartements visités, les trace: In the apartments we visited, traces of water infiltration, damaged materials and partial repairs are visible. Some tenants say they do repairs themselves in the common areas. Others describe problems that have persisted for months, even years.
Dans les espaces communs, les conséquenc: In the common areas, the consequences of the lack of maintenance pile up. Residents took turns guiding us through the desolation. Only Mr. Cherifi speaks openly with his face uncovered. The others prefer to remain anonymous. At 1315 Jules-Poitras Street, a flood in December 2024 left lasting damage in the garage: abandoned vehicles, persistent dampness, no full restoration. Building access is described as faulty. “Anyone can walk in,” says one resident, pointing to unlocked doors and entry codes “that every delivery person knows.”
À cela, il faut ajouter l’existence de n: On top of that, there are many vacant units. Each of the buildings has 76 apartments. According to the defence committee coordinator’s estimates, no more than about thirty apartments per building are occupied, with several units left open or under construction, as we were able to see.
Par ailleurs, La Converse a appris auprè: In addition, La Converse learned from the Montréal Fire Department that firefighters from Station 73 carried out no fewer than 40 interventions in these four buildings between April 2025 and April 2026, also noting a few false alarms.
Marouan Cherifi, représentant du comité: Marouan Cherifi, representative of the tenants’ defence committee, and Nicholas Harvest, spokesperson for Offensive Populaire Montréal. Photo: Offensive populaire
Plusieurs locataires décrivent par aille: Several tenants also describe repeated approaches, often in the form of home visits. According to Marouane Cherifi, a door-to-door phase preceded the sending of official documents. Hired by a subcontracting firm, representatives knocked on tenants’ doors to “explain” the renovation project and offer sums of money to leave. “They come to your place, they tell you the landlord is going to invest millions, that you need to find somewhere else to live, and then they put a figure on the table,” he says.
Des ententes sont alors proposées, avec: Agreements are then offered, with amounts generally ranging from $1,500 to $4,000 for temporarily vacating the premises for announced periods of about five months.
À mesure que la discussion avance, l’app: As the discussion goes on, the approach shifts: “When they sense the person might give in, they ask whether they’d be ready to leave their apartment permanently.”
Ces propositions s’accompagnent de docum: These offers come with documents that some tenants say are hard to understand. On his lawyer’s advice, Mr. Cherifi refuses to sign an agreement that, in his view, would limit available remedies in the event of a dispute. Others say they signed without understanding all the implications, notably because of language barriers. “Some people were given something to sign, but they didn’t understand it,” says a neighbour.
Plusieurs locataires rencontrés lors de: Several tenants we met during our visit describe a more diffuse climate of pressure. They report repeated visits, sometimes without clear notice, vaguely announced technical interventions, and attempts to enter apartments. “They say they’ll come by during the week, without giving a specific time,” says one resident, who says they lost several days of work waiting.
Ces pratiques s’inscrivent, selon les té: According to the accounts gathered, these practices take place in a context where living conditions keep getting worse. For some, this accumulation makes it hard to stay. “At some point, people leave,” sums up one tenant.
<strong>Offensive populaire et émergence: Offensive populaire and the emergence of a defence committee
Mais certains choisissent de rester, et: But some choose to stay, and their mobilization took shape at the start of spring. Several dozen residents from the four buildings took part in a first assembly. At the end of the meeting, a defence committee was formed, with an elected representative to coordinate communications and structure the steps to take. “We had to centralize the information and respond collectively,” explains Marouane Cherifi, chosen by his neighbours to play that role.
Le collectif Offensive Populaire – Montr: The collective Offensive Populaire – Montréal then got involved in the neighbourhood. The activist group went door to door, prepared assemblies and offered organizational support. Its spokesperson, Nicholas Harvest, describes its approach as an attempt to build local responses to housing conflicts. “We don’t show up with a ready-made solution. Mostly, we try to create the conditions for tenants to organize among themselves and decide collectively what they want to do,” he explains. In practical terms, the collective helps organize the first meetings, supports the spread of information and encourages coordinated actions.
Sur le terrain, cette implication coïnci: On the ground, this involvement coincides with a change of scale. Tenants no longer respond alone to the landlord’s offers: collective refusals are issued, trips to the borough council are organized, and information circulates between buildings. “We started acting together,” sums up one resident.
Cette organisation reste toutefois ancré: This organizing nonetheless remains rooted in the neighbourhood. Several tenants we met stress that a dynamic had emerged among neighbours before outside supporters arrived. Offensive Populaire acts as a relay and a framework, without replacing the residents. In a few weeks, this combined effort by residents and activists has built real leverage where before there had only been scattered efforts.
<strong>Orem Capital : entre discours de: Orem Capital: between the language of renovation and accelerated revaluation
Dans un avis transmis aux locataires le: In a notice sent to tenants on January 20, 2026, obtained by La Converse, Orem Capital presents its intervention as a necessary operation. The company cites a “lack of maintenance by the former owner” and announces major work aimed at ensuring “the safety of occupants” and providing a “comfortable and lasting” living environment. Plumbing, electrical, windows, balconies – the announced renovation is comprehensive. The document also states that tenants can stay in place or be temporarily relocated, but warns them that there will be service interruptions and disturbances due to the construction.
Du côté des locataires, on associe toute: Tenants, however, link this work to a broader transformation of the rental stock. One case comes up again and again: that of a resident whose rent will go from $860 to $1,800 after the work planned for July. For Offensive Populaire’s spokesperson, it’s obvious: “What we’re seeing here isn’t an isolated case. It’s a logic where decay and renovations become levers to transform a rental stock and change who lives in it.”
Cette logique est observée dans un autre: This logic can be seen in another building in the area, 1310 Quenneville Street, which was emptied, renovated and recently put up for rent. In a call we made to ask about availability, the agent on the line told us that rents for a 4½ started at $1,600. That’s double. The old rents, still in effect in the neighbouring buildings, ranged between $800 and $1000.
La Converse a communiqué à plusieurs rep: La Converse contacted Orem Capital several times to get its side of the story. A response deadline was granted before publication, but the company never replied.
<strong>Quand la Ville s’en remet aux tr: When the City defers to the courts
Les documents municipaux montrent que la: Municipal documents show that the deterioration of the Chameran buildings has been known for several years. As early as 2024, inspections found unsanitary conditions, water infiltration and the presence of vermin, leading to notices of non-compliance sent to the former owner. In this context, the residents we met voiced their great fear: that of not being able to return after the work. Many see the ongoing renovations as part of a renoviction strategy, backed up by the rent increases seen in neighbouring buildings already put back on the market.
Interrogé au sujet de ces inquiétudes, l: Asked about these concerns, borough mayor Alan DeSousa does not accept this reading of the facts and says the City intervenes “when there are complaints” to enforce bylaws. On the question of rent increases and evictions, he consistently refers to the Administrative Housing Tribunal (TAL). “It’s the TAL that decides whether an increase is compliant,” he stresses to La Converse.
Et quand on lui parle d’une possible gen: And when asked about possible gentrification of the neighbourhood, the Saint-Laurent mayor prefers to emphasize the City’s role in informing tenants about their options for recourse.
Pourtant, il est allé écouter les locata: Yet he did go to listen to tenants at their April 4 assembly, organized by Offensive Populaire, and to hear their concerns about the announced work first-hand. A few days later, at the <l1>April 7 borough council meeting</l1>, several dozen tenants went to city hall to challenge the council again. They asked for concrete measures in response to the deterioration of the buildings and the departure notices they had received. But, finding no satisfactory commitment, they left the meeting before it ended, as a sign of discontent.
<strong>Ce que permet (et ne permet pas): What the legal framework allows (and doesn’t allow)
Le Code civil du Québec encadre la procé: The Civil Code of Québec sets out the procedure a landlord must follow in the case of major work (<l1>Arts. 1922 and 1923</l1>). The landlord must send a detailed notice stating the nature of the work and its duration and, if tenants have to vacate, offer compensation covering the tenant’s reasonable expenses. Consulted by La Converse, housing lawyer Ré Poulin-Ladouceur points out that the law provides that evacuation must be at no cost to the tenant, meaning it must cover moving and storage costs, as well as the rent difference if the temporary housing is more expensive. “Tenants are entitled to equivalent housing in the same area, and the difference must be covered by the landlord,” says Poulin-Ladouceur. In their view, the amounts offered in some notices (around $2,600 for five months) appear insufficient. But, based on the documents sent to tenants, Poulin-Ladouceur believes the notice received by the Chameran tenants is not valid. “The notice was signed in March but sent in early April, so less than three months before the start of the work, in violation of Article 1923,” they say. That, they conclude, is fatal to the procedure started by the landlord and will prevent the question of compensation from even being reached.
À quelques semaines de l’échéance, l’atm: A few weeks from the deadline, the atmosphere is electric. In the apartments that are still occupied, those who remain stick together, discuss strategy and refuse the cheques offered by the landlord. “We’re not leaving,” people repeat on Quenneville and Jules-Poitras streets. It is no longer just a question of walls and ceilings; it is a fight for the right to live in one’s own neighbourhood. In Chameran, the fight is only beginning.
Rénoviction à Saint-Laurent : des locata: Renoviction in Saint-Laurent: Chameran tenants refuse to leave their homes despite major work
À Saint-Laurent, des locataires dénoncen: In Saint-Laurent, tenants are denouncing a possible renoviction following notices of major work and are organizing to resist what they see as a disguised eviction
À partir du début d’avril, les soupçons: Starting in early April, suspicions were confirmed when some tenants began receiving notices of major renovations from the Administrative Housing Tribunal (TAL). According to Orem Capital, the new owner, the work would require the units to be vacated for five months, starting July 1<sup>st</sup>, 2026. For the tenants, there is no doubt: this is a classic case of renoviction. So they are organizing to defend themselves against what they see as an imminent threat.
